answers.transcript:
Okay, er, I want to talk about my aunt, she is the sister of my mother.
She is fifty years old and she work in a primary school.
I know her since I am a child, because she live in the same street with us.
Every weekend we go to her house and we eat together, all the family.
She is very patient in many situation, er, for example in her class.
When the children is very noisy she never shout, she only wait and she speak slow.
Also in my family, when we have a big problem, she stay calm and she listen everybody.
My father is not like this, he get angry very fast and after he is sorry.
I think the patience is useful because the people can trust her and they tell her everything.
Er, yes, this is my aunt, she is a very very patient person.

why_this_band.fluency_coherence: The talk runs from start to finish but follows a single pattern: every sentence opens with "she ..." and connectors are limited to and / because / also. All four points on the card are touched on, but each gets only two sentences, and examples are never opened up.
why_this_band.lexical_resource: Word choice does not move beyond the everyday core: patient, calm, angry, problem keep recurring, and emphasis is made with "very very patient". There is not a single idiom or collocation that describes patience.
why_this_band.grammatical_range_accuracy: Most sentences have a subject-verb agreement or tense error (she work, she live, the children is, he get angry, I know her since I am a child), but meaning is never lost. Structures are almost entirely simple sentences; there is no complex structure beyond the two when clauses.

answers.what_would_lift_it: First, open up the card's third point with a real event — tell one scene from start to finish, whether in the classroom or in the family. Then fix agreement errors of the "she work / she live" kind, since these are spread across every sentence of the response.

answers.transcript:
So I'd like to talk about my aunt Nesrin, who is my mother's younger sister, and honestly she's the most patient person that I know.
I've known her all my life, obviously, because we lived in the same neighbourhood when I was small, and I used to spend nearly every weekend in her flat.
She's a teacher in a primary school, so I think her job also taught her a lot of patience.
When the children in her class are making noise, she doesn't shout at all, she just waits, she waits until they become quiet, and after that she starts the lesson again with a very soft voice.
My mother says that she has a very big patience, even with people who really deserve to be shouted.
And in the family it's the same thing.
Last year my cousin had a big problem in his university and everybody was giving him advice at the same time, but my aunt only listened him, I think for two hours, and she didn't say anything.
I think this is useful because people trust her, and, er, they can tell her things that they cannot tell to other persons.
That's why I admire her a lot.

why_this_band.fluency_coherence: The response is long and develops all four points on the card, but the flow catches here and there: repetitions such as "she just waits, she waits until" and simple transitions such as "and after that", "and in the family it's the same thing". The cousin example is well chosen but is left without being tied to an outcome.
why_this_band.lexical_resource: There is enough vocabulary to describe the topic comfortably (neighbourhood, advice, soft voice, admire), but collocation slips: "she has a very big patience", "deserve to be shouted", "other persons". No idiom is used, and the delivery stays flat.
why_this_band.grammatical_range_accuracy: A relative clause, used to, the past continuous and time clauses are formed with ease, and most sentences are error-free. The remaining errors sit in a narrow set: tense agreement in reported speech (he said that I have to), dropped prepositions (listened him, tell to other persons).

answers.what_would_lift_it: Tie the cousin story to an outcome: say not what the aunt did but what those two hours changed. On the vocabulary side, drop literal translations such as "big patience" and move to a natural collocation such as "she never loses her patience".

answers.transcript:
Right, so the person I've chosen is my aunt Nesrin, my mum's younger sister, and she's easily the most patient person in our family.
I've known her my whole life, obviously. We lived a couple of streets apart when I was growing up, so I was round at her place most weekends, and I suppose I've watched her deal with, well, a lot of situations that would have finished me off.
She teaches seven-year-olds, which I think would test anyone's patience, but she genuinely takes it all in her stride.
If the class is completely wild, she won't raise her voice, she'll just stand at the front and wait them out, and somehow that works far better than shouting ever does.
Where it really shows, though, is with my grandmother. She's got quite forgetful over the last few years and she'll ask the same question maybe ten times in an afternoon, and my aunt answers it every single time as if she's hearing it for the first time. I'd have lost my temper hours earlier, to be honest.
And why I think that patience is useful, well, it's that people end up telling her things.
There's a lot of people in our family who ring her when something's gone wrong, because she doesn't jump straight in with advice and she doesn't judge you. She just keeps a level head and lets you talk yourself round to it.
Which is rarer than you'd think, actually.

why_this_band.fluency_coherence: A self-propelling narrative: the topic is built in the order the speaker chooses and turns with their own markers, such as "Where it really shows, though, is with my grandmother". There is one self-correction ("I've watched her deal with, well, a lot of situations"), the rare kind of correction that eight lines allow.
why_this_band.lexical_resource: Idiomatic material is plentiful and exactly in place: takes it all in her stride, wait them out, raise her voice, lost my temper, keeps a level head, jump straight in with advice, talk yourself round. The spoken register is consistent (round at her place, to be honest).
why_this_band.grammatical_range_accuracy: Structural range is wide: a conditional clause, a relative clause, an as if structure, would have + past participle. Errors are rare and specific to speech ("There's a lot of people" — a common agreement slip in speech), costing the listener nothing.

answers.what_would_lift_it: This response is on target; for the next level up, the assessment in the grandmother example needs to be taken one step further to also describe the cost of the patience (what it costs the aunt). There is nothing left to do in the language.
